what_its_for: Dasatinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of blood cancer called chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and a certain type of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It works by blocking signals inside cancer cells that tell them to grow and multiply, helping to slow or stop the cancer.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food. Do NOT crush, cut, or chew the tablet. Take it at the same time every day to help you remember. If you vomit shortly after taking your dose, do not take another tablet — wait until your next scheduled dose.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your type of cancer and your body's response to treatment. The usual adult dose ranges from 70 mg to 140 mg once or twice daily. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions and never change your dose on your own. Your doctor may adjust your dose if you have side effects.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular scheduled time. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store dasatinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep this medicine away from moisture, heat, and direct sunlight. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking dasatinib, as it can increase the amount of drug in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Avoid St. John's Wort (an herbal supplement) as it can make dasatinib less effective. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking any antacids — if you need one, take it either 2 hours before or 2 hours after your dasatinib dose. Avoid becoming pregnant while on this medication, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for some time after stopping. Avoid breastfeeding while taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: shortness of breath or trouble breathing, chest pain or tightness, sudden weight gain or swelling in your legs, ankles, or feet, severe headache or vision changes, unusual bleeding or bruising, blood in your urine or stool, black or tarry stools, coughing up blood, signs of infection such as fever (temperature above 100.4°F / 38°C), chills, or sore throat, skin rash or blistering, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or severe stomach pain. Also contact your doctor if you feel unusually tired, dizzy, or have fainting spells.
when_it_works: Dasatinib starts working soon after you begin taking it, but it may take several weeks to months before your doctor can confirm it is working through blood tests and checkups. Most patients begin to see improvement in their lab results within the first 3 months of treatment. Keep taking your medicine every day even if you feel well — stopping treatment without your doctor's approval can allow the cancer to come back.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use dasatinib if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 30 days after your last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Children: Dasatinib can be used in some children with certain types of leukemia; the dose will be carefully calculated by the doctor based on the child's weight. Older adults (65 and over): Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as fluid buildup and fatigue. Regular monitoring by your doctor is important. Kidney or Liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease before starting this medication, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
